hacker_news.title: Show HN: Robotics needs better CAD, so I wrote a B-rep kernel and 3,487 tests
hacker_news.description: Hey HN, I’m Tony. I’m a co-founder of Springcraft, where we have been doing a lot of CAD modeling for robot parts. Our team kept running into limitations with existing kernels, and so I decided to write a new B-rep kernel and a new comprehensive, kernel-agnostic B-rep conformance test suite. Both are available today under MIT licenses. The kernel, springrep, is written in safe Rust with no dependencies. It covers a broad range of our mechanical CAD needs, including advanced fillets, sweeps, lofts, shells, offsets, STEP and exact measurements and queries. Claude Code made it feasible to write this, but it took a lot of time and care to get it right. The test suite, brep-conformance, has 3,487 cases covering the modeling operations common across kernels: booleans, fillets, chamfers, shells, offsets, sweeps, lofts, STEP, and queries with expected answers coming from closed forms and exact geometry. It caught hundreds of bugs, edge cases, and hot spots in springrep that our own tests had missed, and now springrep passes all of it. We’ve also run it on a few popular open-source kernels and anyone can run it on theirs. This is the first version, so there are surely mistakes in the test and adapters. Corrections, pull requests, and new kernels are welcome. kernel: https://github.com/springcraft-ai/springrep conformance suite: https://springcraft-ai.github.io/brep-conformance/

hacker_news.title: Launch HN: Maritime (YC F26) – A managed cloud for production AI agents
hacker_news.description: Hi HN, we're Ary and Maria, co-founders of Maritime ( https://maritime.sh ). We're building an agent-native cloud that handles everything from custom environments to lifecycle management for AI agents. Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lCWMdBQ96rY There’s been an explosion of sandbox companies coming out of SF, but sandboxes solve maybe 10% of the infrastructure problem for AI agents. The approach that most sandboxing companies take is: You buy Hetzner/OVH Cloud bare metal servers, use Firecracker to slice the servers up into VMs, sell those VMs with low margins. It’s a bit of an oversimplification, but the point is it’s a narrow solution to a fairly difficult problem. We talked to a couple hundred companies that are building AI agents. From personal assistants and coding agents to specialized healthcare agents, and the main pattern we saw was that even after choosing a sandbox provider, you still have to build additional infrastructure just to get things working. These were the primary points of friction: 1. Agent lifecycle management. There’s a lot that you have to build in order to properly give your agents VMs: things like sleep/wake, persistent storage, triggers, scheduling, per-user routing and spend caps, health monitoring, failure recovery, and deploying updates across thousands of VMs without downtime. There are so many of these small sandbox management tasks that companies have to build and maintain themselves, and they add up. 2. Custom environments. Production agents have varying needs. Some agents need Windows applications. Others need Android, browsers with persistent sessions, custom operating system images, preinstalled desktop software and applications, or specific dependencies. Some agents need access to private networks to interact with customer-specific things on prem, or residential IPs, or the ability to restrict network access completely. 3. Cost optimization. If you’re selling a personal assistant for $20/month, a sandbox that costs $0.04/hour comes out to roughly $29/month if you keep it running continuously, not including LLM inference, storage, etc. There is a way to combat this though, which is to optimize sandbox usage with auto-snapshotting, making things event-driven, mounting S3 buckets to agent environments via FUSE for cheap storage, cold-tiering snapshots, etc. All roads lead to… building more infrastructure. So what did we build differently? We give each agent its own isolated, persistent microVM and a configurable environment. On top of the compute, we built a lot of composable services: provisioning, persistent state, sleep/wake orchestration, triggers, schedule creation, monitoring, network configuration, updates, rollbacks, recovery, per-agent spend tracking, login handoffs, all the things you’d need for production agents. We also spent a huge amount of time optimizing cost. A lot of thought was put into things such as scale-to-zero, copy-on-write over shared base images, compressed memory snapshots, hot/warm/cold snapshot and disk tiering, and other optimizations while balancing these with performance metrics like latency. As a result, Maritime costs $1 for a 2gb RAM agent per month (unlimited usage for that $1), with additional resources available as needed. Maria was a visiting lecturer at MIT and did research at Project NANDA on agent infrastructure. Ary did research on agent coordination protocols at the same lab. We started Maritime together this March because of all the issues we faced with trying to deploy agents to the cloud during our research. We want your feedback. If you're building an agent product, what did you have to build on top of sandboxes to make them work? We want to know about all the workarounds and weird things you’ve had to build. Are there things you’ve tried to build with VMs but couldn’t? Does Maritime fit your needs? Is there a feature we’re missing that would make us more enticing? Happy to answer any questions in the comments. https://maritime.sh

hacker_news.title: Show HN: Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we use to build Mastra
hacker_news.description: Hi HN, we're Shane, Sam, and Abhi. Almost two years ago, we shared Mastra, our open-source TypeScript agent framework, on Show HN: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43103073 . It got a few hundred upvotes; a couple of weeks later our downloads had doubled, and we were off to the races. Today we're sharing Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we built to help maintain Mastra itself. At Mastra, we now average nearly 4M downloads per week, and with Factory our team now merges hundreds of PRs a week across the mastra-ai GitHub org. Last week, Factory opened and merged 238 PRs, alongside 630 merged PRs from humans. There's a lot of debate about what a software factory is. For us Factory is a configurable agentic kanban board that's @-taggable in Slack. Under the hood, it uses Mastra’s durable agents for long-running sessions, our conversational memory system, a markdown based wiki with source citations to incorporate company knowledge, signals that subscribe to PR comments wired up into sessions, and a customizable cloud sandbox with our coding harness (working on supporting Claude Code, Codex etc). When we started out, we modeled Factory around our existing workflow-oriented process (triage, plan, build, review, shipped). Three months later, we find ourselves mostly driving it through Slack vs a web UI. We’ve seen more senior engineers kick off sessions in parallel (“triage the 20 oldest issues and let’s evaluate…”). We’re using bug and vuln scanners now, and we’ve closed our repo to outside contributors, asking folks to write detailed issue repros instead. You can get started with `npm create factory`. It’s fully open-source, so you can run it entirely on your infra (we also offer a hosted version). Comment here, we would love to know what you think! https://factory.mastra.ai https://github.com/mastra-ai/template-factory
